Mình vừa viết một bài trong series Inside ClaudeKit: khi nào dùng `/ck:plan --deep --tdd` cho refactor lớn.

Điểm dễ nhầm là hai option này không cùng loại.

🔹 `--deep` là mode, đổi pipeline planning. Nó bắt plan soi kỹ scope, file inventory, dependency giữa các phase, test gap.
🔹 `--tdd` là flag, thêm flow tests-first. Viết test chụp behavior hiện tại trước khi refactor, rồi dùng nó làm regression gate.
🔹 Bật cả cặp khi task vừa rộng, vừa có behavior cũ cần giữ. Ví dụ tách billing module nhưng vẫn phải giữ retry, idempotency, webhook replay, status transition.
🔹 Task nhỏ vài file thì dùng `--fast` hoặc default. Greenfield thì đừng ép `--tdd` cho có.

Ý mình thích nhất trong bài: plan kỹ không phải để "nghĩ nhiều cho sang", mà để cook bớt đoán. Với refactor lớn, đoán sai scope ở đầu thường đắt hơn vài lượt scout.

Bài có decision matrix, template prompt, pitfalls và phần Inside mổ xẻ `--deep`/`--tdd` hoạt động ra sao.

New Inside ClaudeKit post: when to use `/ck:plan --deep --tdd`.

The important distinction:

• `--deep` is a mode. It changes the planning pipeline: architecture research, per-phase scout, red-team review, validation, file inventory, dependency map.
• `--tdd` is a flag. It composes with any mode and changes execution order: test current behavior first, refactor second, run a concrete regression gate.

Use both for major refactors where scope is wide and existing behavior must survive.

Example: extracting a billing module while preserving retry rules, idempotency, webhook replay, invoice status transitions, and frontend API contracts.

Don't use both for tiny fixes or greenfield work. The overhead is real, and there is no existing behavior for `--tdd` to snapshot.

Full post covers the decision matrix, prompt templates, and the subtle bug where `--tdd` can accidentally preserve a known bug as "current behavior."

I published a new Inside ClaudeKit writeup on a planning choice that shows up often in larger refactors: when to use `/ck:plan --deep --tdd`, and when the shorter path is better.

The short version: `--deep` and `--tdd` solve different risks.

`--deep` is a mode. It changes the planning pipeline so the agent spends more time mapping the work before implementation: architecture research, affected areas, per-phase scout, file inventory, dependency map, test gaps, red-team review, and validation.

`--tdd` is a flag. It composes with any mode and changes the order of execution: write tests that capture current behavior first, refactor second, then run a concrete regression gate.

They pair well when the task has both problems at once:

• The scope is wide enough that a normal plan may miss files, jobs, migrations, or API contracts
• Existing behavior must survive the refactor
• The module has stateful or async behavior, such as retry rules, idempotency, webhook replay, status transitions, or background jobs

The running example in the post is extracting a billing module from a monolith. That kind of task touches API routes, database schema, payment jobs, admin UI, shared contracts, and edge cases that are easy to break after the happy path still passes.

The post also covers when not to use the combo: small fixes, greenfield code, unclear approaches that need `/ck:brainstorm` first, or cases where the known bugs should be fixed before a tests-first refactor.

Main takeaway: `--deep` gives the map. `--tdd` gives the regression gate. Use both when being wrong late would cost more than planning carefully up front.
